stem: A rectangular wire loop with sides $l_1 = 0.5\ \mathrm{m}$, $l_2 = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ is removed with constant velocity $v = 3\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$ parallel to its longer sides from a region of constant magnetic field $B_0 = 1\ \mathrm{T}$ perpendicular to its plane (see Figure). The loop's electrical resistance is $R = 1.5\ \Omega$. Find the current in the loop as a function of the distance $x$ of its leading edge from the boundary of the field region.
stem_lead: A rectangular wire loop with sides $l_1 = 0.5\ \mathrm{m}$, $l_2 = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ is removed with constant velocity $v = 3\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$ parallel to its longer sides from a region of constant magnetic field $B_0 = 1\ \mathrm{T}$ perpendicular to its plane (see Figure). The loop's electrical resistance is $R = 1.5\ \Omega$. Find the current in the loop as a function of the distance $x$ of its leading edge from the boundary of the field region.

mark_scheme.text:
Let $x$ be the distance of the leading side of the loop from the boundary. The flux through the loop is
\[ \Phi = B_0 l_1 (l_2 - x) \]
for $0 < x < l_2$. For $x < 0$ the whole loop is in the field and $\Phi = B_0l_1l_2$ is constant; for $x > l_2$ the flux is zero. Hence the flux changes only for $0 < x < l_2$, and there it induces an emf
\[ \mathcal{E} = -\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = -B_0l_1\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = -B_0l_1v . \]

stem: A plane conducting circular wire loop lies perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B$, and its area $S(t)$ is changed as $S(t) = S_0(1 - \alpha t)$ for $0 < t < 1/\alpha$ ($S_0, \alpha$ constant). The wire has resistance per unit length $\rho\ \Omega\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Find the current in the wire.
stem_lead: A plane conducting circular wire loop lies perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B$, and its area $S(t)$ is changed as $S(t) = S_0(1 - \alpha t)$ for $0 < t < 1/\alpha$ ($S_0, \alpha$ constant). The wire has resistance per unit length $\rho\ \Omega\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Find the current in the wire.

mark_scheme.text:
The flux is $\Phi = BS(t) = BS_0(1-\alpha t)$, so the induced emf is constant, $\mathcal{E} = |\mathrm{d}\Phi/\mathrm{d}t| = S_0 B\alpha$, with its direction fixed by Lenz's law. The loop's resistance is $R = 2\pi r(t)\rho$ with $r(t) = [S(t)/\pi]^{1/2}$, so
\[ I(t) = \frac{\alpha B}{2\rho}\left[\frac{S_0}{\pi(1-\alpha t)}\right]^{1/2}. \]

This produces a current $I = \mathcal{E}/R$ and the dissipated power is $P = \mathcal{E}^2/R = 1.2\times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{W}$. The total work done is $W = Pt = 1.2\times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{J}$.

She wears a necklace enclosing area $A = 0.01\ \mathrm{m^2}$ of field and having a resistance $r = 0.01\ \Omega$. stem_lead: A physicist works in a laboratory where the magnetic field is $B_1 = 2\ \mathrm{T}$. She wears a necklace enclosing area $A = 0.01\ \mathrm{m^2}$ of field and having a resistance $r = 0.01\ \Omega$. Because of a power failure, the field decays to $B_2 = 1\ \mathrm{T}$ in a time $t = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}$. Estimate the current in her necklace and the total heat produced.

mark_scheme.text: $\Delta\Phi = (B_1 - B_2)A$, so the induced emf is $\mathcal{E} = \Delta\Phi/t = 1\times 0.01/0.001 = 10\ \mathrm{V}$. The current is $I = \mathcal{E}/r = 1000\ \mathrm{A}$, the dissipated power is $P = \mathcal{E}I = 10^{4}\ \mathrm{W}$ and the total heat produced is $Pt = 10\ \mathrm{J}$. While this is not large, it is extremely localized, and the very high current $I = 1000\ \mathrm{A}$ is very dangerous. People working in regions of high magnetic field are strongly advised not to wear any conducting loops (e.g. bangles, rings).

stem: To measure the field $B$ between the poles of an electromagnet, a small test loop of area $A = 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, resistance $R = 10\ \Omega$ and $N = 20$ turns is pulled out of it. A galvanometer shows that a total charge $Q = 2\times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}$ passed through the loop. What is $B$?
stem_lead: To measure the field $B$ between the poles of an electromagnet, a small test loop of area $A = 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, resistance $R = 10\ \Omega$ and $N = 20$ turns is pulled out of it. A galvanometer shows that a total charge $Q = 2\times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}$ passed through the loop. What is $B$?

mark_scheme.text:
The flux through the loop was $\Phi = NBA$ and was reduced to zero in time $t$, so the induced emf is $\mathcal{E} = NBA/t$. The current is $I = \mathcal{E}/R = NBA/(Rt)$ and the total charge passed was $Q = It = NBA/R$, so
\[ B = \frac{QR}{NA} = \frac{2\times 10^{-6}\times 10}{20\times 10^{-4}} = 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{T} \]
with the data given.

stem: A coil carries a current of $I = 10\ \mathrm{A}$. When the circuit is broken the current decays to zero in a time $\Delta t = 0.25\ \mathrm{s}$. The inductance of the coil is $L = 18$ Henry. What is the average induced emf?
stem_lead: A coil carries a current of $I = 10\ \mathrm{A}$. When the circuit is broken the current decays to zero in a time $\Delta t = 0.25\ \mathrm{s}$. The inductance of the coil is $L = 18$ Henry. What is the average induced emf?

mark_scheme.text:
The self-induced emf is $V = L\,\Delta I/\Delta t$. Here the current collapses all the way to zero, so $\Delta I = I = 10\ \mathrm{A}$, and
\[ V = 18 \times \frac{10}{0.25} = 720\ \mathrm{V}. \]

mark_scheme.text:
The flux linkage is $N\Phi$, so
\[ L = \frac{N\Phi}{I} = \frac{100 \times 10^{-5}}{5} = 2 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{H} = 0.2\ \mathrm{mH}. \]

stem: A rectangular loop of conducting wire has area $A$ and $N$ turns. It is free to rotate about an axis of symmetry. A constant magnetic field $B$ is present and perpendicular to the axis. Find the induced emf as a function of time if the loop is rotated at angular velocity $\omega$.
stem_lead: A rectangular loop of conducting wire has area $A$ and $N$ turns. It is free to rotate about an axis of symmetry. A constant magnetic field $B$ is present and perpendicular to the axis. Find the induced emf as a function of time if the loop is rotated at angular velocity $\omega$.

mark_scheme.text:
Measuring $t$ from the instant at which the loop normal is parallel to $\mathbf{B}$, the normal makes an angle $\theta = \omega t$ with the field and the flux linkage is
\[ \Phi = NAB\cos\omega t. \]
Expanding $\Phi + \Delta\Phi = NAB\cos\omega(t+\Delta t) = NAB(\cos\omega t\cos\omega\Delta t - \sin\omega t\sin\omega\Delta t)$ and using $\cos\omega\Delta t \approx 1$, $\sin\omega\Delta t \approx \omega\Delta t$ for small $\Delta t$ leaves the change in the flux over $\Delta t$. stem: Oil is added to the right-hand arm of a U-tube containing water. The oil floats above the water to a height of $h = 10\ \mathrm{cm}$. The top of the oil $+$ water column is a height $d = 2\ \mathrm{cm}$ above the top of the water column in the other arm (see Figure). Calculate the oil density $\rho_0$. Fluid of density $\rho_x$ is added to the water column in the left arm to a height $l = h/2$. If the fluid levels in the two arms are now equal, calculate $\rho_x$.
stem_lead: Oil is added to the right-hand arm of a U-tube containing water. The oil floats above the water to a height of $h = 10\ \mathrm{cm}$. The top of the oil $+$ water column is a height $d = 2\ \mathrm{cm}$ above the top of the water column in the other arm (see Figure). Calculate the oil density $\rho_0$. Fluid of density $\rho_x$ is added to the water column in the left arm to a height $l = h/2$. If the fluid levels in the two arms are now equal, calculate $\rho_x$.

mark_scheme.text:
Balancing the oil column against the water that stands beside it,
\[ \rho_0 h g = \rho_w (h-d) g \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \rho_0 = \rho_w \frac{h-d}{h} = 0.8\rho_w = 800\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}. \]
With the second fluid added the levels are equal, so the oil column of height $h$ balances a column of the same height that is half water and half fluid $x$:
\[ \rho_0 g h = \rho_w g \frac{h}{2} + \rho_x g \frac{h}{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \rho_x = 2\rho_0 - \rho_w = 1600 - 1000 = 600\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}. \]

stem: A hydraulic press contains oil of density $\rho_0 = 800\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, and the areas of the large and small cylinders are $A_l = 0.5\ \mathrm{m^2}$, $A_s = 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$. The mass of the large piston is $M_l = 51\ \mathrm{kg}$, while the small piston has an unknown mass $m$. If an additional mass $M = 510\ \mathrm{kg}$ is placed on the large piston, the press is in balance with the small piston a height $h = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ above the large one (see Figure). stem_lead: A hydraulic press contains oil of density $\rho_0 = 800\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, and the areas of the large and small cylinders are $A_l = 0.5\ \mathrm{m^2}$, $A_s = 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$. The mass of the large piston is $M_l = 51\ \mathrm{kg}$, while the small piston has an unknown mass $m$. If an additional mass $M = 510\ \mathrm{kg}$ is placed on the large piston, the press is in balance with the small piston a height $h = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ above the large one (see Figure). Find the mass $m$.

mark_scheme.text:
Equating the pressure just below the large piston to the pressure a height $h$ higher, just below the small one,
\[ \frac{(M+M_l)g}{A_l} = \frac{mg}{A_s} + \rho_0 g h, \]
so that
\[ m = (M+M_l)\frac{A_s}{A_l} - \rho_0 h A_s = 561 \times (10^{-4}/0.5) - 800 \times 1 \times 10^{-4} = 0.032\ \mathrm{kg}. \]

stem: How could you decide if a wedding ring is made of pure gold using sensitive scales, a liquid volume measure, a length of thread, and a sample of pure gold?
stem_lead: How could you decide if a wedding ring is made of pure gold using sensitive scales, a liquid volume measure, a length of thread, and a sample of pure gold?

mark_scheme.text: Any impurity alloyed with the gold changes the density of the metal, almost always lowering it, so density is the property to test. Weigh the ring on the scales to get $m_{\text{ring}}$. Fill the volume measure to the brim, lower the ring into it on the thread, and take the ring out again on the thread: the liquid now missing from the measure has the volume $V_{\text{ring}}$ of the ring. Then $\rho_{\text{ring}} = m_{\text{ring}}/V_{\text{ring}}$. Doing exactly the same to the sample of pure gold gives $\rho_{\text{ref}}$ by the same method, so no tabulated value is needed and the two results can be compared directly: if $\rho_{\text{ring}} = \rho_{\text{ref}}$ the ring is pure gold, and if it is lower the ring is alloyed. (Archimedes is said to have been led to his principle by exactly this kind of experiment, asked by the King of Syracuse to determine the purity of his crown.)

mark_scheme.text:
(a) Standing, the weight $Mg$ is spread over both soles, of area $\approx 2bl$, so $P \approx Mg/2bl \approx 16{,}800\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$.
(b) Lying flat, the weight is spread over an area $\approx hw$, so $P \approx Mg/hw \approx 820\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$. A hard floor is uncomfortable because far less of the body actually touches it than touches a bed, so on those few contact patches the pressure is much higher.
On stiletto heels, $A = 2\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$ and $P = Mg/A \approx 3\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ -- even static pressures of this order are enough to damage floors.

stem: The tires on a racing bicycle are inflated to a pressure $P = 7\ \mathrm{atm}$. Does the pressure gauge on the pump read $7\ \mathrm{atm}$? The combined mass of the bicycle and rider is $m = 70\ \mathrm{kg}$. What is the total tire area in contact with the road?
stem_lead: The tires on a racing bicycle are inflated to a pressure $P = 7\ \mathrm{atm}$. Does the pressure gauge on the pump read $7\ \mathrm{atm}$? The combined mass of the bicycle and rider is $m = 70\ \mathrm{kg}$. What is the total tire area in contact with the road?

mark_scheme.text:
No. A pressure gauge measures the \emph{excess} pressure $P - P_A$, so it reads $6\ \mathrm{atm}$; before inflation it reads zero although the pressure inside the tire is then $P_A$. In equilibrium the road pushes up with $P = 7P_A$ per unit area of contact, but $1P_A$ of that merely balances the atmosphere pressing down from above, so the weight is carried by the excess $6P_A$:
\[ 6P_A A = mg, \qquad A = \frac{mg}{6P_A} = \frac{70 \times 9.8}{6\times10^{5}} = 1.1\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2} = 11\ \mathrm{cm^2}. \]

stem: Two cylinders of cross-sectional area $A = 10\ \mathrm{m}^2$ are fitted smoothly together as shown in the Figure, and then evacuated. Masses $M$ are hung from cables attached to each of the cylinders. How large can the masses $M$ be made before the cylinders are pulled apart?
stem_lead: Two cylinders of cross-sectional area $A = 10\ \mathrm{m}^2$ are fitted smoothly together as shown in the Figure, and then evacuated. Masses $M$ are hung from cables attached to each of the cylinders. How large can the masses $M$ be made before the cylinders are pulled apart?

mark_scheme.text:
The cylinders are held together only by the atmospheric pressure acting on their outer cross-sections. At the largest $M$ the reaction force between the two faces has just vanished, so for one cylinder $\Sigma F_x = 0$ reads
\[ A P_A = Mg, \]
since each cable carries tension $T = Mg$. Hence
\[ M = \frac{A P_A}{g} = \frac{10 \times 10^{5}}{9.8} = 1.02\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{kg} \simeq 102\ \mathrm{tonnes}. \]
For any other shape only the projected cross-sectional area matters. This is the Magdeburg-hemispheres experiment, in which teams of horses could not prise apart a pair of evacuated hemispheres.

stem: A payload $m = 200\ \mathrm{kg}$ is held stationary by a balloon at a certain height above the ground. The volume of the balloon is $V_b = 1000\ \mathrm{m}^3$, and is far larger than that of the payload. Express the gas density $\rho_b$ inside the balloon in terms of the air density $\rho_a$ at this height.
stem_lead: A payload $m = 200\ \mathrm{kg}$ is held stationary by a balloon at a certain height above the ground. The volume of the balloon is $V_b = 1000\ \mathrm{m}^3$, and is far larger than that of the payload. Express the gas density $\rho_b$ inside the balloon in terms of the air density $\rho_a$ at this height.

mark_scheme.text:
Buoyancy must balance the total weight of gas plus payload:
\[ \rho_b V_b g + mg = \rho_a V_b g, \]
so
\[ \rho_b = \rho_a - \frac{m}{V_b} = \rho_a - 0.2\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}. \]
This is possible only if $\rho_a > \rho_{\mathrm{crit}} = 0.2\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$: the balloon cannot be lifted to a height at which the air density is lower than $m/V_b$, which is effectively the average density of balloon and payload together.

stem: Early airships were filled with hydrogen rather than with helium, sometimes with tragic consequences (e.g. the destruction by fire of the German airship \emph{Hindenburg} in 1937). One sometimes reads that the reason for using hydrogen was that, since the density $\rho_{\mathrm{He}}$ of helium is twice that of hydrogen ($\rho_{\mathrm{H}}$) under the same conditions, twice the volume of helium would have been needed to lift the same payload. Is this correct? ($\rho_{\mathrm{H}} = 0.09\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, air density $\rho_a = 1.3\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.)
stem_lead: Early airships were filled with hydrogen rather than with helium, sometimes with tragic consequences (e.g. the destruction by fire of the German airship \emph{Hindenburg} in 1937). One sometimes reads that the reason for using hydrogen was that, since the density $\rho_{\mathrm{He}}$ of helium is twice that of hydrogen ($\rho_{\mathrm{H}}$) under the same conditions, twice the volume of helium would have been needed to lift the same payload. Is this correct? ($\rho_{\mathrm{H}} = 0.09\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, air density $\rho_a = 1.3\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.)

mark_scheme.text:
No. Lift depends on the \emph{difference} between the air density and the gas density, not on the gas density itself. Requiring the displaced air to carry both payload and gas gives
\[ M = V_{\mathrm{H}}(\rho_a - \rho_{\mathrm{H}}) = V_{\mathrm{He}}(\rho_a - \rho_{\mathrm{He}}), \]
so
\[ \frac{V_{\mathrm{He}}}{V_{\mathrm{H}}} = \frac{\rho_a - \rho_{\mathrm{H}}}{\rho_a - \rho_{\mathrm{He}}} = \frac{1.3 - 0.09}{1.3 - 2\times0.09} = 1.08. \]
The volumes are not very different -- about 8\% larger, not twice as large. The main reason for using hydrogen was the difficulty and expense of producing so much helium.

stem: A ball of uniform density $2/3$ of that of water falls vertically into a pond from a height $h = 10\ \mathrm{m}$ above its surface. How deep below the surface can the ball sink before buoyancy forces push it back? (Neglect the water drag on the motion of the ball.)
stem_lead: A ball of uniform density $2/3$ of that of water falls vertically into a pond from a height $h = 10\ \mathrm{m}$ above its surface. How deep below the surface can the ball sink before buoyancy forces push it back? (Neglect the water drag on the motion of the ball.)

mark_scheme.text:
Above the surface the ball is in free fall, so it enters the water with speed $v = (2gh)^{1/2}$. Once fully submerged the resultant upward force is $F = \rho_w V g - \rho_b V g$, and with mass $m = V\rho_b$ the upward acceleration is
\[ a = \frac{F}{m} = \left(\frac{\rho_w}{\rho_b} - 1\right)g = 0.5g. \]
Using $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ay$ with $v_0 = -(2gh)^{1/2}$, the downward motion stops ($v = 0$) at
\[ y = -\frac{v_0^2}{2a} = -\frac{2gh}{2a} = -2h = -20\ \mathrm{m}, \]
i.e. the ball reaches a depth of $20\ \mathrm{m}$, twice the height of the drop.

stem: A yacht is at rest on a small lake. What happens to the water level if the yachtsman throws overboard (a) a buoy, and (b) an anchor?
stem_lead: A yacht is at rest on a small lake. What happens to the water level if the yachtsman throws overboard (a) a buoy, and (b) an anchor?

mark_scheme.text:
(a) By Archimedes' principle the buoy displaces its own weight of water whether it is inside the yacht or floating beside it, so the water level remains unchanged.

(b) The anchor also displaces its own weight of water while it is inside the boat, but less once it sinks: on the bottom it displaces only its own \emph{volume} of water, which weighs less than the anchor does. So the water level drops.

stem: A plastic cube of density $\rho = 800\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ and side $a = 5\ \mathrm{cm}$ is floated in a cylindrical water container of surface area $A = 100\ \mathrm{cm}^2$. Find the resulting increase $h$ of the water height. A mass $m$ is placed on the cube and just submerges it. Find $m$.
stem_lead: A plastic cube of density $\rho = 800\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ and side $a = 5\ \mathrm{cm}$ is floated in a cylindrical water container of surface area $A = 100\ \mathrm{cm}^2$. Find the resulting increase $h$ of the water height. A mass $m$ is placed on the cube and just submerges it. Find $m$.

mark_scheme.text:
Floating: $a^2 x \rho_w = a^3\rho$, so $x = (\rho/\rho_w)a = 0.8 \times 0.05 = 0.04\ \mathrm{m}$ and the displaced volume is $V_s = a^2x = (0.05)^2 \times 0.04 = 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3}$. The level therefore rises by
\[ h = \frac{V_s}{A} = \frac{10^{-4}}{10^{-2}} = 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m} = 1\ \mathrm{cm}. \]
With the mass $m$ on top the cube is just fully submerged, so $V\rho_w g = V\rho g + mg$ and
\[ m = (\rho_w - \rho)V = (1000 - 800)(0.05)^3 = 0.025\ \mathrm{kg} = 25\ \mathrm{g}. \]

stem_lead: A cube of side $a$ is made of material of density $\rho = 3\rho_w/4$, where $\rho_w$ is the density of water. It is placed in a container with a square cross-section whose side is $a + c$, where $c \ll a$, and whose height exceeds $a$ (see Figure). Find the minimum volume $V$ of water that must be poured into the container to float the cube. Can $V$ be made arbitrarily small by reducing $c$?

mark_scheme.text:
The cube has mass $M = 3a^3\rho_w/4$ and floats once it displaces a mass $M$ of water, which (since $c \ll a$ makes the container's base area very close to $a^2$) requires the water to reach a height $h = 3a/4$. Counting only the thin water around the four sides,
\[ V \simeq 4 \times a h \frac{c}{2} = \frac{3}{2}a^2 c. \]
Yes: $V$ becomes arbitrarily small as $c$ is decreased, because the pressure at a given depth below the surface of a continuous body of fluid is exactly the same no matter how little of it there is. In practice the lower limit is reached when there is so little water that surface tension breaks it up and it is no longer a continuous fluid.

stem: A certain liquid has density $\rho$, and surface tension $\gamma$ and contact angle $\theta$ when in contact with glass and air. Find the height $h$ of the liquid in a glass tube of cylindrical radius $r$ immersed in this liquid.
stem_lead: A certain liquid has density $\rho$, and surface tension $\gamma$ and contact angle $\theta$ when in contact with glass and air. Find the height $h$ of the liquid in a glass tube of cylindrical radius $r$ immersed in this liquid.

mark_scheme.text:
The upward force exerted by surface tension is $F_t = 2\pi r \gamma \cos\theta$, and it must balance the weight $W = \pi r^2 h \rho g$ of the raised column. Setting $F_t = W$,
\[ h = \frac{2\gamma\cos\theta}{\rho g r}. \]

stem: Can capillary action account for sap rising in trees? (Assume surface tension of sap is $\gamma = 0.07\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, contact angle $\theta = 0$, sap density $\rho = 10^3\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, tree capillary radius $= 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mm}$.)
stem_lead: Can capillary action account for sap rising in trees? (Assume surface tension of sap is $\gamma = 0.07\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, contact angle $\theta = 0$, sap density $\rho = 10^3\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, tree capillary radius $= 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mm}$.)

mark_scheme.text:
Using $h = 2\gamma\cos\theta/(\rho g r)$ with $\theta = 0$, surface tension can hold a column of sap of height
\[ h = \frac{2\times 0.07}{10^3 \times 9.8 \times 10^{-5}} = 1.4\ \mathrm{m}. \]
As trees grow considerably taller than this, capillary action cannot be significant.

stem: A glass tube has a removable cap at one end, which tends to fall off when the tube is inverted. The cap is made of material of density $\rho = 700\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{-3}}$ and is $d = 2\ \mathrm{mm}$ thick. For what tube radii $r$ will wetting the end of the tube keep the cap on when it is inverted? (Assume surface tension of water $\gamma = 0.07\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$ and contact angles $\theta = 0$ where appropriate.)
stem_lead: A glass tube has a removable cap at one end, which tends to fall off when the tube is inverted. The cap is made of material of density $\rho = 700\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{-3}}$ and is $d = 2\ \mathrm{mm}$ thick. For what tube radii $r$ will wetting the end of the tube keep the cap on when it is inverted? (Assume surface tension of water $\gamma = 0.07\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$ and contact angles $\theta = 0$ where appropriate.)

mark_scheme.text:
With a thin film of water in the gap, the surface-tension force $F_t = 2\pi r\gamma$ must balance the cap's weight $mg = \pi r^2 d\rho g$ together with the rim's reaction $R$, so $2\pi r\gamma = \pi r^2 d\rho g + R$, i.e.
\[ r = \frac{2\gamma}{d\rho g} - \frac{R}{\pi r d\rho g}. \]
Since $R$ is positive, the largest $r$ is given by $R = 0$, i.e. when the surface tension force just balances the weight of the cap. This gives
\[ r_{\mathrm{max}} = \frac{2\gamma}{d\rho g} = \frac{2\times 0.07}{2\times10^{-3}\times 700\times 9.8} = 0.01\ \mathrm{m} = 1\ \mathrm{cm}, \]
so the cap is held on for tube radii up to about $1\ \mathrm{cm}$.

stem:
The pressures inside and outside a spherical membrane of radius $r$ are $P_i$, $P_o$, with $P_i > P_o$. Show that the material of the membrane must exert total tension per unit length $t$, where
\[ P_i - P_o = \frac{2t}{r}. \]
If the material is a liquid whose \emph{surface} tension is $\gamma$, show that
\[ P_i - P_o = \frac{4\gamma}{r}. \]
stem_lead:
The pressures inside and outside a spherical membrane of radius $r$ are $P_i$, $P_o$, with $P_i > P_o$. Show that the material of the membrane must exert total tension per unit length $t$, where
\[ P_i - P_o = \frac{2t}{r}. \]
If the material is a liquid whose \emph{surface} tension is $\gamma$, show that
\[ P_i - P_o = \frac{4\gamma}{r}. \]

mark_scheme.text:
Cut the sphere in half. The net outward pressure force on one hemisphere is $(P_i - P_o)$ times the \emph{projected} area $\pi r^2$, because all components other than the one perpendicular to the cutting plane cancel by symmetry. That force is balanced by the tension in the membrane acting round the cut circle, which by the definition of $t$ is $2\pi r t$. Hence $(P_i - P_o)\pi r^2 = 2\pi r t$, i.e.
\[ P_i - P_o = \frac{2t}{r}. \]
If the membrane is a liquid film it has an inner and an outer surface, each of tension $\gamma$, so the total tension per unit length is $t = 2\gamma$ and
\[ P_i - P_o = \frac{4\gamma}{r}. \]

stem: Repeat the last question for the case of a cylindrical tube of radius $r$. Why do boiling frankfurters tend to split lengthways rather than around their cross-sections?
stem_lead: Repeat the last question for the case of a cylindrical tube of radius $r$. Why do boiling frankfurters tend to split lengthways rather than around their cross-sections?

mark_scheme.text:
For a cylindrical tube the equilibrium of half of a length $l$ of tube gives $2rl(P_i-P_o) = 2lt$, i.e.
\[ P_i - P_o = \frac{t}{r}. \]
If the wall is a liquid film with two surfaces then $t = 2\gamma$, so
\[ P_i - P_o = \frac{2\gamma}{r}. \]
The tension the wall must supply grows with the radius of curvature it has to contain. Along a frankfurter the skin is straight, so that radius is infinite and the hoop tension has to carry the whole pressure difference by itself; this is the largest tension anywhere in the skin, and it is the tension that a lengthways split relieves. So boiling frankfurters split lengthways rather than around their cross-sections.

stem: A tire on a racing bicycle is inflated to a pressure $P_i = 7\ \mathrm{atm}$. The radius of the tire is $r = 1.5\ \mathrm{cm}$. Find the tension in the walls.
stem_lead: A tire on a racing bicycle is inflated to a pressure $P_i = 7\ \mathrm{atm}$. The radius of the tire is $r = 1.5\ \mathrm{cm}$. Find the tension in the walls.

mark_scheme.text:
A short section of the tire is effectively a straight cylinder, so the result of P349 applies: $t = (P_i - P_o)r$. With $P_i = 7\ \mathrm{atm}$ and $P_o = 1\ \mathrm{atm}$ the excess pressure is $6P_A = 6\times 10^5\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, so
\[ t = 6\times 10^5 \times 1.5\times 10^{-2} = 9000\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}. \]

stem: A spherical balloon has interior pressure $P_1$ and radius $r_1$, and is in equilibrium inside an enclosure with pressure $P_o = 8P_1/9$. The enclosure is gradually evacuated. Assuming that the temperature is fixed and the tension $t$ per unit length of the balloon material remains constant, show that the balloon radius never exceeds $3r_1$.
stem_lead: A spherical balloon has interior pressure $P_1$ and radius $r_1$, and is in equilibrium inside an enclosure with pressure $P_o = 8P_1/9$. The enclosure is gradually evacuated. Assuming that the temperature is fixed and the tension $t$ per unit length of the balloon material remains constant, show that the balloon radius never exceeds $3r_1$.

mark_scheme.text:
The balloon obeys $P_i - P_o = 2t/r$. Initially $P_i = P_1$, $P_o = 8P_1/9$, $r = r_1$, so $P_1/9 = 2t/r_1$. The largest radius $r_2$ occurs when the enclosure is fully evacuated, $P_o = 0$, giving $P_2 = 2t/r_2$. Dividing,
\[ \frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{9r_2}{r_1}. \]
At fixed temperature $Pr^3$ is constant, so
\[ \frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{r_2^3}{r_1^3}. \]
Comparing the two gives $r_2^2 = 9r_1^2$, i.e. $r_2 = 3r_1$: the balloon radius never exceeds $3r_1$.

stem: The air sacs in the lungs (alveoli) can be approximated as small spherical membranes of radius $r$ containing air at atmospheric pressure $P_0$. The pressure $P_c$ in the chest cavity (pleural pressure) increases when the person breathes out. Simultaneously, muscle contraction decreases $r$. These changes are reversed as the person breathes in. Show that the membrane tension per unit length $t$ must decrease as the person exhales and increase as he inhales.
stem_lead: The air sacs in the lungs (alveoli) can be approximated as small spherical membranes of radius $r$ containing air at atmospheric pressure $P_0$. The pressure $P_c$ in the chest cavity (pleural pressure) increases when the person breathes out. Simultaneously, muscle contraction decreases $r$. These changes are reversed as the person breathes in. Show that the membrane tension per unit length $t$ must decrease as the person exhales and increase as he inhales.

mark_scheme.text:
The membrane is a sphere, so equilibrium requires $(P_0 - P_c)r = 2t$, i.e.
\[ t = \tfrac{1}{2}(P_0 - P_c)\,r. \]
In breathing out, $P_c$ increases while $P_0$ is fixed, so $P_0 - P_c$ decreases; at the same time muscle contraction decreases $r$. Both factors in the product fall, so $t$ must fall. Breathing in reverses both changes, so $t$ must rise. If $t$ did not follow, the alveolus could not stay in equilibrium and would either collapse or rupture; the adjustment is provided by the surfactant protein lining the air sacs.

stem:
Two identical small balloons are inflated, one much more than the other. They are then connected by a pipe which is closed by a valve between them. The whole apparatus is placed in an evacuated enclosure. What happens when the valve is opened?

(You may assume that the surface tension of the balloon material is independent of the balloon's size except when the balloon is smaller than a certain spherical radius $r_{\min}$, below which the surface tension decreases.)
stem_lead:
Two identical small balloons are inflated, one much more than the other. They are then connected by a pipe which is closed by a valve between them. The whole apparatus is placed in an evacuated enclosure. What happens when the valve is opened?

(You may assume that the surface tension of the balloon material is independent of the balloon's size except when the balloon is smaller than a certain spherical radius $r_{\min}$, below which the surface tension decreases.)

mark_scheme.text: One might expect the balloons to equalise in size, but the opposite happens. With the enclosure evacuated each balloon obeys $P_{i1} - P_o = 2t_1/r_1$ and $P_{i2} - P_o = 2t_2/r_2$. While both balloons are larger than $r_{\min}$ the tensions are equal, $t_1 = t_2 = t$, so $r_1 > r_2$ forces $P_{i1} < P_{i2}$: the SMALLER balloon holds the HIGHER pressure. (This is why a balloon is hardest to blow up at the start.) When the valve is opened, air therefore rushes from the small balloon into the large one, making the large one larger and the small one smaller still. The pressures equalise at some common $P_i$ with $P_{i1} < P_i < P_{i2}$, and the two equations then require $t_2/t_1 = r_2/r_1 < 1$ -- so the small balloon must have contracted below $r_{\min}$, where its surface tension has fallen. The apparatus ends with one large balloon and one shrunken one, not two equal ones. The same end state would be reached from two balloons of equal pressure, since the slightest perturbation starts the process off.

stem: A container is filled with water to a depth $H = 2.5\ \mathrm{m}$. The container is tightly sealed and above the water is air at pressure $P_1 = 1.34\times 10^5\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ (see Figure). A small hole is drilled at a height $h = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ above the bottom of the container. What is the speed of the resulting jet of water? Compare your answer with the case of a container open at the top, but otherwise identical.
stem_lead: A container is filled with water to a depth $H = 2.5\ \mathrm{m}$. The container is tightly sealed and above the water is air at pressure $P_1 = 1.34\times 10^5\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ (see Figure). A small hole is drilled at a height $h = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ above the bottom of the container. What is the speed of the resulting jet of water? Compare your answer with the case of a container open at the top, but otherwise identical.

mark_scheme.text:
Applying Bernoulli's theorem along a streamline from the water surface (where $v \approx 0$, $P = P_1$, height $H$) to the hole (where $P = P_A$, height $h$),
\[ \frac{P_1}{\rho} + gH = \frac{P_A}{\rho} + \tfrac{1}{2}v^2 + gh, \]
so the jet velocity $v$ is given by
\[ v^2 = 2g(H-h) + 2\,\frac{P_1 - P_A}{\rho}. \]

mark_scheme.text: Mass conservation in steady incompressible flow makes $r = vA$ the same at every cross-section. In MKS units $r = 6\ \mathrm{m^3\,min^{-1}} = 0.1\ \mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, and $A_1 = \pi d_1^2/4 = 0.031\ \mathrm{m^2}$, $A_2 = \pi d_2^2/4 = 0.126\ \mathrm{m^2}$. Hence $v_1 = r/A_1 = 3.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ near the pump, and the water leaves the pipe at $v_2 = r/A_2 = 0.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

stem: A wide container is filled with water up to a depth $H$. A small hole is drilled in the container at a distance $h$ below the water level, and a jet of water emerges from it. How far from the container does the jet hit the ground?
stem_lead: A wide container is filled with water up to a depth $H$. A small hole is drilled in the container at a distance $h$ below the water level, and a jet of water emerges from it. How far from the container does the jet hit the ground?

mark_scheme.text:
Bernoulli along a streamline from the free surface to the hole gives $v = (2gh)^{1/2}$. The jet leaves horizontally and falls a height $H - h$, taking $t = [2(H-h)/g]^{1/2}$. Hence
\[ s = vt = 2\left[h(H-h)\right]^{1/2}. \]
The range is greatest, and equal to $H$, when the hole is about halfway down the filled part of the container, $h \approx H/2$; it is small both for $h \to 0$ (little pressure head to drive the jet) and for $h \to H$ (the jet emerges too close to the ground).

Find $v$ if the difference in mercury levels is $h = 25\ \mathrm{mm}$. (The density of mercury is $\rho_{\mathrm{Hg}} = 13{,}600\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{-3}}$.)
stem_lead: A Venturi tube (see Figure) is used to measure the water speed $v$ in a pipe by comparing the pressures in the wide and narrow sections (cross-sectional areas $A, A' = A/4$). Find $v$ if the difference in mercury levels is $h = 25\ \mathrm{mm}$. (The density of mercury is $\rho_{\mathrm{Hg}} = 13{,}600\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{-3}}$.)

mark_scheme.text:
Bernoulli along the horizontal pipe gives $P + \tfrac12\rho_w v^2 = P' + \tfrac12\rho_w v'^2$, and mass conservation $\rho_w A v = \rho_w A' v'$ gives $v' = v(A/A') = 4v$. Hence $16v^2 - v^2 = 2(P-P')/\rho_w$, i.e. $v^2 = (2/15)\left[(P-P')/\rho_w\right]$. Hydrostatic equilibrium of the mercury requires $P - P' = \rho_{\mathrm{Hg}}gh$, so
\[ v = \left(\frac{2}{15}\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{Hg}}}{\rho_w}gh\right)^{1/2} = \left(\frac{2\times 13{,}600 \times 9.8 \times 2.5\times10^{-2}}{15\times 1000}\right)^{1/2} = 0.67\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}. \]

stem: The window and door of a room are both open. The door opens inwards: why does it tend to slam shut if only slightly ajar?
stem_lead: The window and door of a room are both open. The door opens inwards: why does it tend to slam shut if only slightly ajar?

mark_scheme.text: Let the window and doorway have effective open areas $A_w$ and $A_d$. All the air that enters by the window has to leave by the doorway, so $A_w v_w = A_d v_d$. If the door is only slightly ajar then $A_d < A_w$ and the air must squeeze through the gap at a HIGHER speed, $v_d > v_w$. By Bernoulli's theorem the faster-moving air in the gap is at a LOWER pressure than the slow-moving air in the room, so there is an excess pressure $\Delta P \approx \tfrac12\rho_{\text{air}}\left(v_d^2 - v_w^2\right)$ on the inside face of the door. That excess pushes the door towards the gap, i.e. towards the closed position, and it slams. Opened sufficiently wide the door does not slam: then $A_d$ is comparable with $A_w$, the speed difference is small, and the pressure torque on the door is smaller than the frictional torque at the hinges.

\[ L \approx \frac{1}{2}\left(m^2 - 1\right)\rho v^2 \]
per unit area. Assume that both streamlines pass through A and B.

An airplane of mass $M = 500\ \mathrm{kg}$ has a total wing area $A = 30\ \mathrm{m}^2$, and the airfoil design is such that $m = 1.1$. Estimate the airplane's minimum takeoff speed at sea level ($\rho = 1\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$). How does this change in high-altitude airports?

mark_scheme.text:
The height difference between the two paths is negligible, so Bernoulli's theorem for the two surfaces gives $\dfrac{P_1}{\rho} + \dfrac{v^2}{2} = \dfrac{P_2}{\rho} + \dfrac{m^2v^2}{2}$, since the flow is steady and both paths take the same time between $A$ and $B$, making the upper speed $mv$. Hence $P_1 - P_2 = \dfrac{m^2-1}{2}\rho v^2 = L$ per unit area, upward. The airplane leaves the ground once $F_L = A(P_1 - P_2)$ exceeds $Mg$, so the minimum takeoff speed satisfies $\tfrac12 A(m^2-1)\rho v^2 = Mg$, i.e.
\[ v^2 = \frac{2Mg}{(m^2-1)A\rho}. \]
With the data given, $v = \left[2\times500\times9.8/(0.21\times30)\right]^{1/2} = 39.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} = 142\ \mathrm{km/h}$. At high-altitude airports $\rho$ is significantly smaller, and by the relation above the takeoff speed has to rise as $\rho^{-1/2}$.

mark_scheme.text: The lift condition of P364, $\tfrac{1}{2}A(m^2-1)\rho v^2 = Mg$, rearranges to $\rho = 2Mg/[(m^2-1)Av^2]$. The airplane can still fly at the lowest density when it flies at its greatest speed, so $\rho_{\mathrm{min}} = 2\times 500\times 9.8/(0.21\times 30\times 70^2) = 0.32$ (printed in the source as $0.32\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}}$). Inverting $\rho = 1\times 10^{-z/H}$ gives $z_{\mathrm{max}} = -H\log_{10}\rho_{\mathrm{min}} = 23{,}000\times 0.50 = 11{,}500\ \mathrm{m} = 11.5\ \mathrm{km}$.

stem: In light of P364 can you suggest why the early airplanes (e.g. the Wright brothers') were all biplanes?
stem_lead: In light of P364 can you suggest why the early airplanes (e.g. the Wright brothers') were all biplanes?

mark_scheme.text: The main problem for early airplanes was the lack of sufficiently powerful engines to produce high takeoff speeds $v$. From equation (1) of S364, $v^2 = 2Mg/[(m^2-1)A\rho]$, we see that $v$ is reduced by making $A$ large. This could have been achieved by increasing the wingspan, but it was difficult to produce a strong wing of great length. The easiest way of increasing $A$ was to stack shorter wings above each other, i.e. biplanes (or triplanes).

stem: Two species of bird are very similar in every respect except that every dimension of one species is on average $l$ times the corresponding dimension of the other. How are their respective takeoff speeds for flight related?
stem_lead: Two species of bird are very similar in every respect except that every dimension of one species is on average $l$ times the corresponding dimension of the other. How are their respective takeoff speeds for flight related?

mark_scheme.text: As in P364 the lift force is $F_L \propto Av^2$, where $A$ is the wing area. At takeoff this just equals the weight $Mg$, where $M$ is the bird's mass. Clearly $A$ scales as $l^2$, while $M$ scales as $l^3$, since the average densities of the species are the same. Thus $F_L \propto Av^2 \propto l^2v^2$, while $Mg \propto l^3$. Therefore $F_L = Mg$ requires $v \propto l^{1/2}$. Larger birds have higher takeoff speeds, and often have to run to achieve the necessary lift (e.g. flamingoes).

stem: A \emph{hydrofoil} boat uses submerged fins with airfoil-type cross-sections to lift the boat largely clear of the water and allow much higher speeds. Find the condition for this to be achieved at water speed $u$ and total hydrofoil area $A_h$, if the water streamline path over the upper surface of the latter is $m$ times longer than over the lower surface and the boat has mass $M$. Show that $A_f$ can be much smaller than the wing area required for takeoff of an airplane of the same mass, even with slower speeds $u$ (compare P364).

mark_scheme.text:
The calculation is the same as in S364 with water in place of air. The condition to lift the boat from the water is
\[ u^2 = \frac{2Mg}{(m^2-1)A_h\rho_w}. \]
The great difference here in comparison with P364 is that $\rho_w$ is 1000 times larger than $\rho$ for air. Thus even with $u$ smaller than an airplane's takeoff speed, $A_h$ can be made much smaller than $A$, i.e. hydrofoils are much smaller than airplane wings.

stem:
When a yacht sails into the wind its sails adopt a curved shape as viewed from above (see Figure). At a suitable angle to the wind direction the air on the concave side of the sails moves much more slowly than that on the convex side. If the average speed of the latter is $w$, the sails have total area $A$, and the yacht steers at angle $\theta$ to the wind direction (see Figure), show that the yacht experiences total wind force
\[ F_1 \approx \frac{A}{2}\rho_a w^2 \sin\theta \]
in the forward direction, where $\rho_a$ is the air density.

The same yacht now sails with the wind more nearly behind it (see Figure: at an angle $\phi < 90^\circ$ from directly astern). If the wind has velocity $w$ and the boat's forward speed is much less than this, find the maximum forward force $F_2$ on the yacht and compare it with $F_1$ in the case $\theta = \phi = 45^\circ$.
stem_lead:
When a yacht sails into the wind its sails adopt a curved shape as viewed from above (see Figure). At a suitable angle to the wind direction the air on the concave side of the sails moves much more slowly than that on the convex side. If the average speed of the latter is $w$, the sails have total area $A$, and the yacht steers at angle $\theta$ to the wind direction (see Figure), show that the yacht experiences total wind force
\[ F_1 \approx \frac{A}{2}\rho_a w^2 \sin\theta \]
in the forward direction, where $\rho_a$ is the air density.

The same yacht now sails with the wind more nearly behind it (see Figure: at an angle $\phi < 90^\circ$ from directly astern). If the wind has velocity $w$ and the boat's forward speed is much less than this, find the maximum forward force $F_2$ on the yacht and compare it with $F_1$ in the case $\theta = \phi = 45^\circ$.

mark_scheme.text:
Applied to the sail, Bernoulli's theorem gives $P_1/\rho_a + \tfrac{1}{2}u^2 = P_A/\rho_a$, where $P_1$ is the pressure on the convex side, $P_A$ is atmospheric pressure and $u \approx w$ is the air speed along the convex side. This produces a force $F = (P_A-P_1)A \approx A\rho_a w^2/2$ acting towards the convex side, and so a force $F_1 = F\sin\theta \approx (A\rho_a w^2/2)\sin\theta$ in the direction of the yacht's motion.

With the wind behind, the sails are best deployed perpendicular to the wind velocity. Since the yacht moves much more slowly than the wind, essentially all the wind's momentum is lost to the boat. Per unit area of sail the wind momentum is $\rho_a w$, arriving at velocity $w$, so the momentum transferred per unit time is $\approx A\rho_a w^2$; by Newton's second law this is the total force. Its forward component is $F_2 \approx A\rho_a w^2\cos\phi$. For $\theta = \phi = 45^\circ$, $\sin\theta = \cos\phi = 1/\sqrt{2}$, so
\[ F_1 \approx \frac{A\rho_a w^2}{2\sqrt{2}},\qquad F_2 \approx \frac{A\rho_a w^2}{\sqrt{2}}, \]
so that $F_1 \approx F_2/2$.

stem: The yacht considered in the last two problems has mass $M$, and the submerged depth is approximately constant along its length $l$. The sails are triangular and the mast has height $l$ also (see Figure). Show that $A_f \approx Mg/\rho l$, and hence that the yacht should be designed to maximize the quantity $l^3/M$ to achieve high speeds.
stem_lead: The yacht considered in the last two problems has mass $M$, and the submerged depth is approximately constant along its length $l$. The sails are triangular and the mast has height $l$ also (see Figure). Show that $A_f \approx Mg/\rho l$, and hence that the yacht should be designed to maximize the quantity $l^3/M$ to achieve high speeds.

mark_scheme.text:
By Archimedes' principle, the weight of the boat is equal to that of the water displaced, i.e. $Mg \approx A_f l\rho$. Also the sail area is $A = l^2/2$. Substituting for $A_f$, $A$ into (1, 2) of the previous solution shows that for any angles $\theta$, $\phi$
\[ v_1, v_2 \propto \left(\frac{l^3\rho_a}{M}\right)^{1/2} w. \]
Since $\rho_a$, $w$ are fixed, high sailing speeds are achieved by making $l^3/M$ as large as possible. Long slender yachts are much faster than short stubby ones.

stem: A yacht, as considered in the previous three problems, resists sideways motions by means of its keel, which gives the boat total side-on cross-sectional area $A_s$. Show that the boat should be designed so that $A_s \gg A_f$. What is the usual way of achieving this?
stem_lead: A yacht, as considered in the previous three problems, resists sideways motions by means of its keel, which gives the boat total side-on cross-sectional area $A_s$. Show that the boat should be designed so that $A_s \gg A_f$. What is the usual way of achieving this?

mark_scheme.text: The drag force resisting the sideways motion is $\approx A_s\rho s^2$, where $s$ is the sideways velocity component. Equating this to the sideways forces $F_1\cos\theta$, $F_2\sin\phi$ (cf. S369) shows that $s$ will be as small as possible if $A_s\rho \gg A\rho_a$. To give high forward speed, equations (1, 2) of S370 show that $A\rho_a$ should be as large as possible in comparison with $A_f\rho$. These two requirements are only compatible if $A_s \gg A_f$. Again we see that an efficient yacht should be slender. $A_s$ is made large in practice by making the keel deep, as this also gives stability against the tendency of the wind pressure on the sails to push the boat over.

stem:
A certain Grand Prix racing car has mass $m = 1000\ \mathrm{kg}$, and the coefficient of sliding friction between its tires and the road is $\mu = 0.5$. What is the maximum speed at which it can take a level bend of radius of curvature $r = 100\ \mathrm{m}$?

A very efficient wing of area $A = 2\ \mathrm{m^2}$ is now fitted to the car, so that the air passing above the wing moves much more slowly than the car's speed $v$, while that passing below moves at $v$. What is the new maximum speed around the bend? (Air density $\rho = 1\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{-3}}$.)
stem_lead:
A certain Grand Prix racing car has mass $m = 1000\ \mathrm{kg}$, and the coefficient of sliding friction between its tires and the road is $\mu = 0.5$. What is the maximum speed at which it can take a level bend of radius of curvature $r = 100\ \mathrm{m}$?

A very efficient wing of area $A = 2\ \mathrm{m^2}$ is now fitted to the car, so that the air passing above the wing moves much more slowly than the car's speed $v$, while that passing below moves at $v$. What is the new maximum speed around the bend? (Air density $\rho = 1\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{-3}}$.)

mark_scheme.text:
Friction must supply the centripetal force, $mv^2/r = \mu N$. With no wing $N = mg$, so $v^2(\text{no wing}) = \mu r g$, giving $v = 22.1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} = 80\ \mathrm{km/h}$. With the wing, Bernoulli's theorem $P_A/\rho = P/\rho + \tfrac12 v^2$ gives an extra downforce $A(P_A - P) = \tfrac12 A\rho v^2$, so $N = mg + \tfrac12 A\rho v^2$ and
\[ v^2(\text{wing}) = \frac{\mu m g}{m/r - \mu A\rho/2}, \]
giving $v = 22.7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} = 82\ \mathrm{km/h}$.

stem: Is the wing of the last question more of an advantage on slow, tight corners or fast, relatively gentle ones?
stem_lead: Is the wing of the last question more of an advantage on slow, tight corners or fast, relatively gentle ones?

mark_scheme.text:
Tight corners have small $r$, while gentle ones have large $r$. From equation (1) of the last answer,
\[ v^2(\text{wing}) = \frac{\mu m g}{m/r - \mu A\rho/2}, \]
we see that on gentle corners the ``wing'' term $\mu A\rho/2$ is more nearly comparable to the other term $m/r$ in the denominator, and thus has a greater effect. Wings give less advantage on tight corners because the lower speeds make the Bernoulli effect less important.

stem: A closed container of volume $V_1 = 12$ liters holds a mass $m_1 = 0.858\ \mathrm{kg}$ of oxygen. It is known that the mass of a liter of oxygen at atmospheric pressure is $m_2 = 0.0015\ \mathrm{kg}$ at the same temperature. What is the pressure in the container?
stem_lead: A closed container of volume $V_1 = 12$ liters holds a mass $m_1 = 0.858\ \mathrm{kg}$ of oxygen. It is known that the mass of a liter of oxygen at atmospheric pressure is $m_2 = 0.0015\ \mathrm{kg}$ at the same temperature. What is the pressure in the container?

mark_scheme.text:
The ideal gas law can be written $P = (R/\mu)\rho T$, so at fixed temperature and fixed composition $P/\rho$ is constant, i.e. $PV/m$ is constant. Writing $V_A$ for 1 liter,
\[ \frac{PV}{m_1} = \frac{P_AV_A}{m_2}, \qquad P = \frac{m_1}{m_2}\frac{V_A}{V}P_A = \frac{0.858}{0.0015}\cdot\frac{1}{12}\times 10^5 = 4.77\times 10^6\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}. \]

The volume of hydrogen is $V_H = 1400\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ and the height of the piston is $h = 40\ \mathrm{cm}$ (see Figure). stem_lead: A cylindrical container is enclosed by a piston of mass $m = 21\ \mathrm{kg}$ and holds a mass $m_H = 0.17\ \mathrm{g}$ of molecular hydrogen. The volume of hydrogen is $V_H = 1400\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ and the height of the piston is $h = 40\ \mathrm{cm}$ (see Figure). Find the atmospheric pressure $P_A$ outside the container if the absolute temperature is $T = 300\ \mathrm{K}$.

mark_scheme.text:
Piston equilibrium gives $P_A + mg/S = P_H$ with $S = V_H/h$, so $P_A = P_H - mgh/V_H$. The equation of state gives $P_H = n_HRT/V_H$ with $n_H = 0.17/2 = 0.085\ \mathrm{mol}$, so
\[ P_A = (n_HRT - mgh)\frac{1}{V_H} = (0.085\times 8.31\times 300 - 21\times 9.8\times 0.4)\frac{1}{1400\times 10^{-6}} = 9.26\times 10^4\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}. \]

With the faucet closed $V_1$, $V_2$ contain $n$, $2n$ moles of a certain ideal gas respectively. The faucet is opened and the system allowed to stabilize at constant temperature. Find the number of moles in each container in terms of $n$.

mark_scheme.text: The total amount is conserved, $n_{\mathrm{tot}} = n + 2n = 3n$, spread over the total volume $3V$, so the molar density is $n/V$ everywhere and the common pressure is $P = (n/V)RT$. Applying $PV_i = n_iRT$ to each vessel in turn, $n_1 = PV_1/RT = 2n$ in the larger container and $n_2 = PV_2/RT = n$ in the smaller one. The two amounts have exchanged.

The car is then transported by truck to a warm district, where the temperature is $t = 40^\circ$ C. Is there a danger that the fuel will overflow the tank? (The volume expansion coefficients of the gasoline and the metal of the tank are $\gamma_G = 9 \times 10^{-4}\ {}^\circ\mathrm{C}^{-1}$ and $\gamma_T = 10^{-5}\ {}^\circ\mathrm{C}^{-1}$.

mark_scheme.text: The tank's capacity grows to $V_T' = (1 + \gamma_T\Delta t)V_T = 1.0004\,V_T$, while the fuel grows to $V_G' = (1 + \gamma_G\Delta t)V_G = 1.036\,V_G$. Substituting $V_G = 0.97\,V_T$ gives $V_G' = 1.036 \times 0.97\,V_T = 1.0049\,V_T$. Thus $V_G' > V_T'$ at $40^\circ$ C: the fuel will overflow. Note that this result is independent of the volumes $V_T$, $V_G$ of the tank and gasoline, and depends only on their \emph{relative} size.

stem: A solid has thermal linear expansion coefficient $\alpha$. Show that its volume expansion coefficient is $\gamma = 3\alpha$.
stem_lead: A solid has thermal linear expansion coefficient $\alpha$. Show that its volume expansion coefficient is $\gamma = 3\alpha$.

mark_scheme.text:
Take a cube of side $a$, so $V = a^3$. Under a small rise $\Delta T$ each side becomes $a(1+\alpha\Delta T)$, so
\[V + \Delta V = a^3(1+\alpha\Delta T)^3 \simeq a^3(1+3\alpha\Delta T)\]
since $\alpha\Delta T \ll 1$. By the definition of $\gamma$ this same quantity is $V(1+\gamma\Delta T) = a^3(1+\gamma\Delta T)$, so $\gamma = 3\alpha$.

stem: A steel cube floats in a bath of mercury. What happens as the temperature rises? (Coefficient of linear expansion of steel $= \alpha_s = 1.2\times10^{-5}\ {}^\circ\mathrm{C}^{-1}$, coefficient of volume expansion of mercury $= \gamma_m = 1.8\times10^{-4}\ {}^\circ\mathrm{C}^{-1}$.)
stem_lead: A steel cube floats in a bath of mercury. What happens as the temperature rises? (Coefficient of linear expansion of steel $= \alpha_s = 1.2\times10^{-5}\ {}^\circ\mathrm{C}^{-1}$, coefficient of volume expansion of mercury $= \gamma_m = 1.8\times10^{-4}\ {}^\circ\mathrm{C}^{-1}$.)

mark_scheme.text:
By Archimedes' principle the cube displaces its own mass of mercury, so it floats to a depth $d$ given by $m = a^2\rho d$, i.e. $d = m/(a^2\rho)$. On heating, $a = a_0(1+\alpha_s T)$ while the mercury's density falls to $\rho_0(1+\gamma_m T)^{-1}$, so
\[d = \frac{m}{a_0^2\rho_0}\frac{1+\gamma_m T}{(1+\alpha_s T)^2} \simeq d_0\,\frac{1+\gamma_m T}{1+2\alpha_s T} = d_0\,\frac{1+1.8\times10^{-4}T}{1+2.4\times10^{-5}T},\]
which is $> d_0$ and increases with $T$. The level of the mercury bath rises because of the expansion of the mercury, and the cube floats slightly more deeply than before.

stem: A mass $m_1 = 1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of cold water at temperature $t_1 = 7^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is mixed with a mass $m_2 = 2\ \mathrm{kg}$ of hot water at $t_2 = 37^\circ\mathrm{C}$. You may assume that no heat is exchanged with the surroundings, and that the total volume of water does not change. Find the temperature $t$ of the mixture. Did the total internal energy of the water change? What was the total entropy change?
stem_lead: A mass $m_1 = 1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of cold water at temperature $t_1 = 7^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is mixed with a mass $m_2 = 2\ \mathrm{kg}$ of hot water at $t_2 = 37^\circ\mathrm{C}$. You may assume that no heat is exchanged with the surroundings, and that the total volume of water does not change. Find the temperature $t$ of the mixture. Did the total internal energy of the water change? What was the total entropy change?

mark_scheme.text: With $C_w$ the specific heat of water, conservation of heat energy gives $(m_1+m_2)C_w t = m_1 C_w t_1 + m_2 C_w t_2$, so $t = \dfrac{m_1 t_1 + m_2 t_2}{m_1+m_2} = \dfrac{1\times7 + 2\times37}{3} = 27^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The total internal energy change $\Delta U$ is zero, since both $W$ (the work done) and $\Delta Q = \Delta Q_1 + \Delta Q_2$ (the total heat absorbed) are zero. There is nevertheless a nonzero entropy change $\Delta S = \Delta S_1 + \Delta S_2$ (entropy of mixing), because the heat transfers $\Delta Q_1, \Delta Q_2 = -\Delta Q_1$ are not performed at the same temperature; the second law in the form $T\,\Delta S_1 = m_1 C_w \Delta T$ leads to $\Delta S_1 = m_1 C_w \ln(T/T_1)$, and similarly for the second mass.

stem_lead: The tires on a racing bicycle are generally inflated to pressures $P \approx 6\times$ atmospheric. When the valve is sharply depressed, ice forms around it. Why?

mark_scheme.text: The air in the tire expands and cools adiabatically as it rushes out of the valve. With $P_2 = P_1/6$, $\gamma = 1.4$ (appropriate for air) and $T_1 = 290\ \mathrm{K}$, the adiabatic relation gives $T_2 = 174\ \mathrm{K}$, or $-99\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Water vapour in the surrounding air is chilled far below freezing and deposits as ice on the valve. There is of course very little cool air, so the ice soon disappears. A similar effect causes the tiny cloud of water vapour seen on opening coke or champagne bottles.

stem: Why does rain or snow tend to fall on the windward side of a mountain range? Why is there often a warm dry wind on the other side? (e.g. the Chinook on the eastern side of the Rockies.)
stem_lead: Why does rain or snow tend to fall on the windward side of a mountain range? Why is there often a warm dry wind on the other side? (e.g. the Chinook on the eastern side of the Rockies.)

mark_scheme.text: On the windward side the air is forced to rise; the pressure there is lower, so the moisture-laden air has expanded. The expansion is too rapid for much heat to be lost or gained, so it is effectively adiabatic, and the air cools, causing the water vapour to condense and fall as rain or snow. On the other side the air falls and is adiabatically compressed, so its temperature rises. This gives a warm dry wind. Another example is the F\"ohn north of the Alps.

stem_lead: Consider the balloon of P352 above. If instead of the temperature being fixed, the monatomic gas inside the balloon expands adiabatically, show that its maximum radius is smaller than in P352. Why?

mark_scheme.text:
The derivation of equation (1) is still valid, so
\[ \frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{9r_2}{r_1}, \tag{1} \]
but equation (2) is no longer valid, as the gas now expands adiabatically not isothermally. We replace (2) using the adiabatic relation $PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$. Since $\gamma = 5/3$ for a monatomic gas and $V \propto r^3$, this requires $Pr^5 = \text{constant}$, so (2) is replaced by
\[ \frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{r_2^5}{r_1^5}. \tag{2'} \]
Eliminating $P_1/P_2$ between (1) and (2$'$) now gives $r_2 = \sqrt{3}\,r_1$ as opposed to $r_2 = 3r_1$ in the isothermal case. The greater expansion in that case results from the fact that energy is being fed into the gas there to keep its temperature constant. This meant that more work could be done expanding the balloon against the tension in the walls.

stem_lead: A certain mass of ideal gas, with constant-volume specific heat $C_V = 0.6\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, is cooled at constant pressure $P_0 = 10^5\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$. As a result its volume decreases from $V_1 = 1\ \mathrm{m^3}$ to half of this value. Find the amount of heat lost by the gas in this process.

mark_scheme.text: At constant pressure the relevant heat capacity is $C_P = C_V + R$, so $\Delta Q = nC_P\Delta T = \left(\dfrac{C_V}{R}+1\right)(nRT_2 - nRT_1) = \left(\dfrac{C_V}{R}+1\right)P_0(V_2-V_1) = \left(\dfrac{0.6}{8.31}+1\right)10^5(0.5-1) = -5.36\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$. The negative sign shows that heat has been lost by the gas, so the heat lost is $5.36\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$.

The pressure throughout is $P = 1.52\times10^5\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$. Calculate the initial and final temperatures $T_1$, $T_2$ of the gas, the total amount of heat $Q$ absorbed in the process, and the change $\Delta S$ in the entropy of the gas.

mark_scheme.text: $T_1 = PV_1/nR = 274.3\ \mathrm{K}$ and $T_2 = PV_2/nR = 640.2\ \mathrm{K}$. With $\Delta U = \tfrac{3}{2}nR\Delta T = 3R\Delta T$ and $\Delta W = P(V_2-V_1) = nR\Delta T = 2R\Delta T$, the first law gives $Q = \Delta U + \Delta W = 5R(T_2 - T_1) = 5\times8.31\times(640.2-274.3) = 1.52\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$. The entropy change is $\Delta S = \tfrac{3}{2}nR\ln(T_2/T_1) + nR\ln(V_2/V_1) = 3\times8.31\ln(640.2/274.3) + 2\times8.31\ln(0.07/0.03) = 35.2\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.

stem: Two solid bodies of equal masses $m$ and temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2 = 2T_1$ are brought into contact. If their heat capacities are $C_1$ and $C_2 = 1.5C_1$, what is their common temperature, $T$, when they reach thermal equilibrium? Find the entropy change $\Delta S$ for each body, and show that the total entropy of the system has increased. Express your results in terms of $T_1$, $C_1$ and $m$.
stem_lead: Two solid bodies of equal masses $m$ and temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2 = 2T_1$ are brought into contact. If their heat capacities are $C_1$ and $C_2 = 1.5C_1$, what is their common temperature, $T$, when they reach thermal equilibrium? Find the entropy change $\Delta S$ for each body, and show that the total entropy of the system has increased. Express your results in terms of $T_1$, $C_1$ and $m$.

mark_scheme.text: Energy conservation gives $0 = mC_1(T - T_1) + 1.5mC_1(T - 2T_1)$, so $T = 1.6T_1$. The entropy changes are $\Delta S_1 = mC_1\ln(T/T_1) = mC_1\ln 1.6 = 0.47mC_1$ and $\Delta S_2 = 1.5mC_1\ln(T/2T_1) = 1.5mC_1\ln 0.8 = -0.335mC_1$. Their sum $\Delta S = \Delta S_1 + \Delta S_2 = +0.135mC_1 > 0$, as the second law requires: the body with the smaller $T$ is the one with $\Delta Q > 0$, and in $\Delta S = \Delta Q/T$ a given heat carries more entropy at the lower temperature.

Calculate the final volume $V_2$ and temperature $T_2$ of the oxygen. What quantity of work $\Delta W$ is performed in the compression, and what is the change $\Delta U$ of internal energy?

mark_scheme.text: With $m_M = 32\ \mathrm{g}$ for $\mathrm{O_2}$, $n = 160/32 = 5\ \mathrm{mol}$, so $V_1 = nRT_1/P_1 = 5\times8.31\times300/10^5 = 0.125\ \mathrm{m^3}$. For a diatomic gas $\gamma = 7/5$, and $P_1V_1^{\gamma} = P_2V_2^{\gamma}$ gives $V_2 = (P_1/P_2)^{1/\gamma}V_1 = (0.1)^{5/7}\times0.125 = 0.024\ \mathrm{m^3}$. Then $T_2 = (V_1/V_2)^{\gamma-1}T_1 = (0.125/0.024)^{2/5}\times300 = 580\ \mathrm{K}$. The process is adiabatic, so $\Delta S = 0$ and $\Delta U = -\Delta W$: all the compression work goes into internal energy. For a diatomic gas $U = \tfrac{5}{2}nRT$, so $\Delta U = \tfrac{5}{2}nR\Delta T = 2.5\times5\times8.31\times(580-300) = 2.91\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$, which is also the work done in the compression.

Express the changes $\Delta P, \Delta T, \Delta U, \Delta S$ in terms of the initial values $P_0, T_0, U_0, S_0, V_0$ and $n$, the number of molar masses of gas. (Use the formula $\Delta W = nRT\ln(V/V_0)$ for the work done by an isothermal ideal gas in expanding from volume $V_0$ to $V$).
stem_lead: The volume of an ideal gas is doubled in a quasistatic isothermal process. Find the change in the pressure $P$, temperature $T$, internal energy $U$, and entropy $S$. Express the changes $\Delta P, \Delta T, \Delta U, \Delta S$ in terms of the initial values $P_0, T_0, U_0, S_0, V_0$ and $n$, the number of molar masses of gas. (Use the formula $\Delta W = nRT\ln(V/V_0)$ for the work done by an isothermal ideal gas in expanding from volume $V_0$ to $V$).

mark_scheme.text: $\Delta T = 0$ because the process is isothermal. At fixed $T$, $PV = P_0V_0$, so $P = P_0(V_0/V) = P_0/2$ and $\Delta P = -P_0/2$. The internal energy of a fixed mass of ideal gas depends only on $T$ [$U = (3/2)nRT$], so $\Delta U = 0$. With $\Delta U = 0$ the first law gives $Q = \Delta W$, and for a quasistatic process $Q = T\Delta S$, so $\Delta S = \Delta W/T = nR\ln(V/V_0) = nR\ln 2 = 0.693nR$.

subtopic_label: Describe qualitatively, in terms of particles, the effect on the pressure of a f
stem: The gas in a cylinder is adiabatically compressed by a piston. By considering microscopic processes, explain qualitatively why its temperature and pressure rise.
stem_lead: The gas in a cylinder is adiabatically compressed by a piston. By considering microscopic processes, explain qualitatively why its temperature and pressure rise.

mark_scheme.text: As the piston moves inwards, molecules that bounce off it rebound faster. In the frame of a piston advancing at speed $u$, a molecule approaching with axial speed $v_x + u$ is elastically reflected at the same speed $v_x + u$, so in the laboratory frame it leaves with $v_x + 2u$. Intermolecular collisions then share this extra energy through the gas, raising the rms speed $v$ and hence the temperature. Because the compression is adiabatic, none of this energy escapes to the surroundings, so it all stays in the gas: the piston does work against the gas pressure and this work heats the gas. The pressure rises because the momentum transferred per collision, and the rate of collisions, both increase.

stem: A box containing gas is weighed on a scale. Most of the gas molecules are not in contact with the base. Why does the scale nevertheless register the weight of the gas as well as the box?
stem_lead: A box containing gas is weighed on a scale. Most of the gas molecules are not in contact with the base. Why does the scale nevertheless register the weight of the gas as well as the box?

mark_scheme.text: The gas molecules at the base have on average gained kinetic energy $mgh$ compared with those at the top, which have the higher potential energy. This raises the pressure at the base by $Nmgh = \rho g h$, where $N$ is the number of molecules per unit volume -- precisely the amount required to bear the total weight of the gas. Hence the full weight of the gas registers on the scale. The same argument shows that the pressure at every height in the gas is exactly that required to support the weight of the gas above that height.

mark_scheme.text: Setting the rms speed equal to the escape speed in $v = (3kT/\mu m_H)^{1/2}$ gives \[ T = \frac{\mu m_H v_{\mathrm{esc}}^2}{3k}. \] Lighter compounds therefore escape at lower temperatures. With the data given, $v = 27.8\,T^{1/2}\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$ for oxygen, and reaching $v_{\mathrm{esc}}$ requires $T = 1.6\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{K}$. Similarly for nitrogen $T = 1.4\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{K}$, and for hydrogen $T = 1\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{K}$. This difference is important in explaining why the Earth has lost most of the hydrogen in its original atmosphere but retains the oxygen and nitrogen.

stem: A candle is placed a distance $s = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ along the axis of a convex spherical mirror of curvature radius $R = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ (see Figure). Find the position, nature, and magnification of the image. Draw a schematic ray diagram.
stem_lead: A candle is placed a distance $s = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ along the axis of a convex spherical mirror of curvature radius $R = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ (see Figure). Find the position, nature, and magnification of the image. Draw a schematic ray diagram.

mark_scheme.text:
The focal length of a convex mirror is $f = -R/2 = -0.5\ \mathrm{m}$. The formula $1/s - 1/s' = 1/f$ gives
\[ \frac{1}{s'} = \frac{1}{1.5} + \frac{1}{0.5} = \frac{8}{3}, \]
so $s' = 0.375\ \mathrm{m}$: the image is $0.375\ \mathrm{m}$ behind the mirror. The magnification is $m = s'/s = 0.375/1.5 = 0.25$, so the image is virtual, upright and smaller.

stem: An object is on the axis of a concave spherical mirror of curvature radius $R = -2\,\mathrm{m}$. Its image is twice the object size and appears in front of the mirror. Find the positions of the object and image, and supply a ray diagram.
stem_lead: An object is on the axis of a concave spherical mirror of curvature radius $R = -2\,\mathrm{m}$. Its image is twice the object size and appears in front of the mirror. Find the positions of the object and image, and supply a ray diagram.

mark_scheme.text:
The mirror has focal length $f = -R/2 = 1\ \mathrm{m}$. The image is in front of the mirror, so $s' < 0$, and $|s'/s| = 2$ gives $s' = -2s$. Substituting in $1/s - 1/s' = 1/f$:
\[ \frac{1}{s} + \frac{1}{2s} = 1, \]
so $s = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ and $s' = -2s = -3\ \mathrm{m}$. Since $m = s'/s < 0$, the image is real and inverted, $3\ \mathrm{m}$ in front of the mirror.

stem_lead: An object is placed at a distance $s = R/4$ from a concave spherical mirror of curvature radius $R$. Find the position and nature of the image. Draw a ray diagram.

mark_scheme.text:
With $f = R/2$ and $s = R/4$, the mirror formula $1/s - 1/s' = 1/f$ reads
\[ \frac{4}{R} - \frac{1}{s'} = \frac{2}{R}, \]
so $1/s' = 2/R$ and $s' = R/2$. The image lies a distance $R/2$ behind the mirror, and $m = s'/s = (R/2)/(R/4) = 2$: it is virtual, upright and twice the size of the object.

stem: A point light source is a height $h = 50\ \mathrm{cm}$ above a table. An experimenter wishes to obtain a sharp image of the source at the table, using a converging lens of focal length $f = 8\ \mathrm{cm}$. At what height $x$ should she place the lens?
stem_lead: A point light source is a height $h = 50\ \mathrm{cm}$ above a table. An experimenter wishes to obtain a sharp image of the source at the table, using a converging lens of focal length $f = 8\ \mathrm{cm}$. At what height $x$ should she place the lens?

mark_scheme.text: With $s = h - x$ and $s' = x$ the lens formula $\dfrac{1}{h-x} + \dfrac{1}{x} = \dfrac{1}{f}$ becomes, in centimetres, $x^2 - 50x + 400 = 0$, whose roots are $x_1 = 40\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $x_2 = 10\ \mathrm{cm}$. Both heights give a sharp image on the table: interchanging them simply interchanges $s$ and $s'$, which appear symmetrically in the lens formula. At $x = 40\ \mathrm{cm}$ the object distance is $10\ \mathrm{cm}$ and the magnification is $4$; at $x = 10\ \mathrm{cm}$ the object distance is $40\ \mathrm{cm}$ and the magnification is $0.25$.

stem:
Show that the thin lens formula can be rewritten as
\[ pp' = f^2, \]
where $p, p'$ are the distances of the object and image from the first and second focal points.
stem_lead:
Show that the thin lens formula can be rewritten as
\[ pp' = f^2, \]
where $p, p'$ are the distances of the object and image from the first and second focal points.

mark_scheme.text:
By definition $p = s - f$ and $p' = s' - f$, so
\[ pp' = (s-f)(s'-f) = ss' - (s+s')f + f^2. \]
Multiplying the thin lens formula $\dfrac{1}{s} + \dfrac{1}{s'} = \dfrac{1}{f}$ through by $ss'f$ gives $s'f + sf = ss'$, i.e. $ss' = (s+s')f$. The first two terms therefore cancel and
\[ pp' = f^2, \]
which is Newton's form of the thin lens formula.

stem:
Two thin lenses of focal lengths $f_1, f_2$ are placed in contact. Show that they are equivalent to a thin lens with focal length $f$ given by
\[ \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2}. \]
stem_lead:
Two thin lenses of focal lengths $f_1, f_2$ are placed in contact. Show that they are equivalent to a thin lens with focal length $f$ given by
\[ \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2}. \]

mark_scheme.text:
Send in a parallel beam, so that the object for the first lens is at infinity. Putting $s = \infty$ in $1/s + 1/s' = 1/f_1$ gives $s'_1 = f_1$: the focal length of a lens is just the image position for an object at infinity. That image is the object for the second lens, and because the lenses touch, $s_2 = -s'_1 = -f_1$. Then
\[ \frac{1}{s_2} + \frac{1}{s'_2} = \frac{1}{f_2} \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{1}{s'_2} = \frac{1}{f_2} + \frac{1}{f_1}. \]
But $s'_2$ is the image position of the whole pair for an object at infinity, i.e. the focal length $f$ of the combination. Hence
\[ \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2}. \]

stem: Two lenses of power $P_1 = 2$ diopters and $P_2 = 0.5$ diopters are placed in contact. What is the power of the combined lens?
stem_lead: Two lenses of power $P_1 = 2$ diopters and $P_2 = 0.5$ diopters are placed in contact. What is the power of the combined lens?

mark_scheme.text: The power is $1/f$, where $f$ is the focal length, and is measured in diopters (metres$^{-1}$) if $f$ is in metres. By the previous answer the powers of lenses placed in contact simply add, so the combined lens has power $P = P_1 + P_2 = 2.5$ diopters.

stem:
An optical doublet is formed from two lenses A, B made of glass of different refractive indices $n_A, n_B$. Lens A has two convex sides of radius of curvature $R$, and lens B has one flat side and one concave side of radius of curvature $R$. Derive an expression for the power of the doublet.

Both refractive indices vary slightly with wavelength as follows: $n_A = 1.50, 1.51, 1.52$ at red, yellow, and blue respectively, while $n_B = 1.60, 1.62, 1.64$ at the same wavelengths. Show that the doublet has constant power at all three wavelengths.
stem_lead:
An optical doublet is formed from two lenses A, B made of glass of different refractive indices $n_A, n_B$. Lens A has two convex sides of radius of curvature $R$, and lens B has one flat side and one concave side of radius of curvature $R$. Derive an expression for the power of the doublet.

Both refractive indices vary slightly with wavelength as follows: $n_A = 1.50, 1.51, 1.52$ at red, yellow, and blue respectively, while $n_B = 1.60, 1.62, 1.64$ at the same wavelengths. Show that the doublet has constant power at all three wavelengths.

mark_scheme.text:
The lensmaker's formula $P = \dfrac{1}{f} = (n-1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$ gives, for the biconvex lens A and the plano-concave lens B,
\[ P_A = \frac{2(n_A-1)}{R}, \qquad P_B = -\frac{(n_B-1)}{R}, \]
and since the powers of lenses in contact add,
\[ P = P_A + P_B = \frac{1}{R}\left[2n_A - n_B - 1\right]. \]
With the data given, $2(1.50)-1.60-1 = 0.40$, $2(1.51)-1.62-1 = 0.40$ and $2(1.52)-1.64-1 = 0.40$, so $P = 0.4/R$ at all three wavelengths. Doublets are often used to correct chromatic aberration, i.e. the variation of focal length with colour.

stem: A simple camera has a converging lens of focal length $f = 5\ \mathrm{cm}$ and is used to record sharp images of distant objects on film. If instead the objects are $s = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ from the lens, by how much must the distance between the lens and the film be changed?
stem_lead: A simple camera has a converging lens of focal length $f = 5\ \mathrm{cm}$ and is used to record sharp images of distant objects on film. If instead the objects are $s = 1\ \mathrm{m}$ from the lens, by how much must the distance between the lens and the film be changed?

mark_scheme.text: With $s = \infty$ the lens formula gives $s' = f = 5\ \mathrm{cm}$. With $s = 1\ \mathrm{m} = 100\ \mathrm{cm}$, $\frac{1}{s'} + \frac{1}{100} = \frac{1}{5}$, so $s' = 5.26\ \mathrm{cm}$. The lens must be moved $0.26\ \mathrm{cm}$ away from the film.

stem: Show that, except for extreme closeups, the magnification of a camera lens is approximately proportional to the focal length of its lens. How are different magnifications achieved in practice? Does this affect the field of view?
stem_lead: Show that, except for extreme closeups, the magnification of a camera lens is approximately proportional to the focal length of its lens. How are different magnifications achieved in practice? Does this affect the field of view?

mark_scheme.text: If $s \gg f$ then $1/s + 1/s' = 1/f$ gives $s' \approx f$, so the magnification is $m = -s'/s \approx -f/s$: at fixed object distance $|m|$ is proportional to $f$ (the minus sign means the image is inverted). Different magnifications are therefore obtained by changing the lens, which is why cameras have interchangeable lenses; high magnification needs a long focal length, and such a lens sits further from the film. Since the film frame is the same size whatever lens is used, a higher-magnification lens takes in a smaller field of view.

stem: A photographer uses a camera with an $f/8$ lens and obtains a good picture with an exposure of $0.02\ \mathrm{s}$. The diaphragm is now stopped down to $f/16$ and the lighting conditions remain the same. What exposure is now required?
stem_lead: A photographer uses a camera with an $f/8$ lens and obtains a good picture with an exposure of $0.02\ \mathrm{s}$. The diaphragm is now stopped down to $f/16$ and the lighting conditions remain the same. What exposure is now required?

mark_scheme.text: Going from $f/8$ to $f/16$ halves the effective diameter of the lens and so reduces its area, and with it the rate at which light illuminates the film, by a factor 4. The photographer must therefore increase the exposure time by a factor 4, from $0.02\ \mathrm{s}$ to $t_2 = 0.08\ \mathrm{s}$.

stem: By changing the radii of its converging lens, and thus its focal length, the human eye is able to produce a sharp image on the retina (at a fixed distance from the lens) of objects at any distance from a certain minimum (the ``least distance of distinct vision'', or ``near point'') up to infinity. If the near point is a distance $d_n = 25\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the eye's lens, and the retina is $2.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ behind the lens, by what factor must the eye muscles be able to change the lens's focal length?
stem_lead: By changing the radii of its converging lens, and thus its focal length, the human eye is able to produce a sharp image on the retina (at a fixed distance from the lens) of objects at any distance from a certain minimum (the ``least distance of distinct vision'', or ``near point'') up to infinity. If the near point is a distance $d_n = 25\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the eye's lens, and the retina is $2.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ behind the lens, by what factor must the eye muscles be able to change the lens's focal length?

mark_scheme.text:
The image distance is fixed at $s' = 2.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ while $s$ runs over $d_n < s < \infty$, so $1/s$ runs over $1/d_n > 1/s > 0$. With $1/f = 1/s + 1/s'$ this gives
\[ \frac{1}{2.5} < \frac{1}{f} < \frac{1}{2.5} + \frac{1}{d_n}, \]
and with $d_n = 25\ \mathrm{cm}$, $2.27\ \mathrm{cm} < f < 2.50\ \mathrm{cm}$. The muscles must be able to alter $f$ (and so the radii of curvature of the lens) by a factor $2.5/2.27 = 1.1$, i.e. by about $10\%$.

stem: A normal human eye can produce a sharp image of an object at any distance beyond a near point (about $25\ \mathrm{cm}$, see the previous problem) all the way out to infinity. A certain person has an eye with a normal near point, but is unable to see clearly objects beyond a far point at $d_f = 1\ \mathrm{m}$. How can her vision be corrected?
stem_lead: A normal human eye can produce a sharp image of an object at any distance beyond a near point (about $25\ \mathrm{cm}$, see the previous problem) all the way out to infinity. A certain person has an eye with a normal near point, but is unable to see clearly objects beyond a far point at $d_f = 1\ \mathrm{m}$. How can her vision be corrected?

mark_scheme.text: The person is short-sighted (myopic). Her vision is corrected by a lens placed in front of the eye that takes an object at infinity and forms an image no further away than her far point $d_f$. For that lens $s = \infty$ and $s' = -1\ \mathrm{m}$ (the image must lie in front of the eye so as to serve as an object for the eye's own lens), so the lens formula gives $f = s' = -1\ \mathrm{m}$. This is a diverging lens of power $P = -1$ diopter $(\mathrm{m}^{-1})$.

stem: A man has a near point at $d_n = 0.6\ \mathrm{m}$ from his eyes. What power glasses will bring his near point to $d'_n = 0.25\ \mathrm{m}$?
stem_lead: A man has a near point at $d_n = 0.6\ \mathrm{m}$ from his eyes. What power glasses will bring his near point to $d'_n = 0.25\ \mathrm{m}$?

mark_scheme.text:
The man is long-sighted. An object at $d'_n = 0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ must appear to be at $d_n = 0.6\ \mathrm{m}$, i.e. the glasses must form a virtual image there. With $s = d'_n$ and $s' = -d_n$ the thin-lens formula gives
\[ P = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d'_n} - \frac{1}{d_n} = \frac{1}{0.25} - \frac{1}{0.6} = 2.33\ \text{diopters}, \]
so he needs converging lenses of focal length $f = 0.43\ \mathrm{m}$.

stem: The human eye can distinguish point objects down to angular separations $\theta_0 \approx 5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{rad}$ ($\approx 0.03^\circ \approx 1.7'$). If a person has a near point $d_n = 25\ \mathrm{cm}$, what is the size of the smallest detail that he can pick out?
stem_lead: The human eye can distinguish point objects down to angular separations $\theta_0 \approx 5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{rad}$ ($\approx 0.03^\circ \approx 1.7'$). If a person has a near point $d_n = 25\ \mathrm{cm}$, what is the size of the smallest detail that he can pick out?

mark_scheme.text:
A given detail subtends a larger angle the closer it is brought to the eye, but it cannot be brought closer than the near point and still be seen sharply. So the smallest scale that can be distinguished is the one subtending $\theta_0$ at the near point:
\[ s = \theta_0 d_n = (5 \times 10^{-4})(0.25\ \mathrm{m}) = 1.25 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m} = 0.125\ \mathrm{mm}. \]
This formula is correct only with $\theta_0$ in radians.
