stem: A person with a near point $d_n = 25\ \mathrm{cm}$ uses a converging lens with a power of $10$ diopters to view a very small object. Where must the object be placed with respect to the lens for best results, and how large is the angular magnification?
stem_lead: A person with a near point $d_n = 25\ \mathrm{cm}$ uses a converging lens with a power of $10$ diopters to view a very small object. Where must the object be placed with respect to the lens for best results, and how large is the angular magnification?

mark_scheme.text:
The object is placed just inside the focal point of the lens, i.e. just under $f = 1/D = 10\ \mathrm{cm}$ from it, so that it produces a very distant virtual image which can be viewed with a relaxed eye. The angular magnification is $M = \theta_i/\theta_u$, where $\theta_i$ is the angular size of the image seen through the lens and $\theta_u$ that seen by the unaided eye at the near point. Assuming $h \ll f, d_n$, the Figure gives $\theta_i \approx h/f$ and $\theta_u = h/d_n$, so
\[ M = \frac{d_n}{f} = d_n D = (0.25\ \mathrm{m})(10\ \mathrm{m}^{-1}) = 2.5. \]

mark_scheme.text: The star's radial velocity will oscillate back and forth periodically, so its spectral lines are alternately blue-shifted and red-shifted with the orbital period. The mean value of the radial velocity gives the radial velocity of the centre of mass of the binary system. The amplitude of the radial velocity oscillations, combined with Kepler's laws, can be used to constrain or even measure the masses of the stars of the binary.

stem: Two identical sound sources $A$ and $B$ are $1\ \mathrm{m}$ apart under water and emit sound waves of frequency $\nu = 3500\ \mathrm{Hz}$ in phase with each other. A microphone is placed on a line parallel to $AB$ at a distance $L = 1000\ \mathrm{m}$ from $AB$. Where should it be positioned so that the sound intensity is a local maximum? (Speed of sound in water $= 1500\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$.)
stem_lead: Two identical sound sources $A$ and $B$ are $1\ \mathrm{m}$ apart under water and emit sound waves of frequency $\nu = 3500\ \mathrm{Hz}$ in phase with each other. A microphone is placed on a line parallel to $AB$ at a distance $L = 1000\ \mathrm{m}$ from $AB$. Where should it be positioned so that the sound intensity is a local maximum? (Speed of sound in water $= 1500\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$.)

mark_scheme.text: The wavelength is $\lambda = v_s/\nu = 1500/3500 = 0.4286\ \mathrm{m}$. Maxima occur where the two path lengths differ by a whole number of wavelengths, $d\sin\theta_n = n\lambda$, so with $d = 1\ \mathrm{m}$, $\sin\theta_n = 0.4286\,n$. Only $n = 0, 1, 2$ are possible: $\theta_0 = 0$; $\sin\theta_1 = 0.4286$, $\theta_1 = 25.38^\circ$; $\sin\theta_2 = 0.8572$, $\theta_2 = 59^\circ$. The microphone should therefore be placed at $x_n = L\tan\theta_n$ from the symmetry line, i.e. at $x_0 = 0$, $x_1 = 474.4\ \mathrm{m}$ or $x_2 = 1664\ \mathrm{m}$.

stem: A Young's double slit experiment is performed using light of wavelength $\lambda = 5000\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}}$, which emerges in phase from two slits a distance $d = 3\times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm}$ apart. A transparent sheet of thickness $t = 1.5\times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm}$ is placed over one of the slits. The refractive index of the material of this sheet is $n = 1.17$. Where does the central maximum of the interference pattern now appear?
stem_lead: A Young's double slit experiment is performed using light of wavelength $\lambda = 5000\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}}$, which emerges in phase from two slits a distance $d = 3\times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm}$ apart. A transparent sheet of thickness $t = 1.5\times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm}$ is placed over one of the slits. The refractive index of the material of this sheet is $n = 1.17$. Where does the central maximum of the interference pattern now appear?

mark_scheme.text:
Without the sheet the phase difference on the symmetry line is zero. With the sheet in place the total phase difference is
\[ \Delta\Phi = \Delta\Phi_g + \Delta\Phi_d = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\left[d\sin\theta - \frac{t}{\cos\theta}(n-1)\right], \]
and equating this to zero gives $d\sin\theta\cos\theta = t(n-1)$, i.e.
\[ \sin 2\theta = \frac{2t}{d}(n-1). \]
With the data given, $\sin 2\theta = 0.17$, so $\theta = 4.9^\circ$: the central maximum has moved off the axis by about $4.9^\circ$.

subject: physics
subtopic_label: Decide whether scientific work is being done by a specified force on a specified
stem:
When the force on an object depends on the position of the object, we cannot find the work done by it on the object by simply multiplying the force by the displacement. The reason is that there is no one value for the force-it changes. So, we must find the work in tiny little displacements and then add up all the work results. We effectively say, "Yes, the force varies over any given tiny little displacement, but the variation is so small we can approximate the force as being constant during the displacement." Sure, it is not precise, but if we make the displacements infinitesimal, then our error becomes infinitesimal and the result becomes precise. But, to add an infinite number of work contributions by hand would take us forever, longer than a semester. So, we add them up via an integration, which allows us to do all this in minutes (much less than a semester).

Force $\vec{F}=\left(3 x^2 \mathrm{~N}\right) \hat{\mathrm{i}}+(4 \mathrm{~N}) \hat{\mathrm{j}}$, with $x$ in meters, acts on a particle, changing only the kinetic energy of the particle. How much work is done on the particle as it moves from coordinates $(2 \mathrm{~m}, 3 \mathrm{~m})$ to $(3 \mathrm{~m}, 0 \mathrm{~m})$ ?

stem:
A heavy object can sink into the ground during an earthquake if the shaking causes the ground to undergo liquefaction, in which the soil grains experience little friction as they slide over one another. The ground is then effectively quicksand. The possibility of liquefaction in sandy ground can be predicted in terms of the void ratio $e$ for a sample of the ground:
$$
e=\frac{V_{\text {voids }}}{V_{\text {grains }}} .
$$
Here, $V_{\text {grains }}$ is the total volume of the sand grains in the sample and $V_{\text {voids }}$ is the total volume between the grains (in the voids). If $e$ exceeds a critical value of 0.80 , liquefaction can occur during an earthquake. What is the corresponding sand density $\rho_{\text {sand }}$ ? Solid silicon dioxide (the primary component of sand) has a density of $\rho_{\mathrm{SiO}_2}=2.600 \times 10^3 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^3$.
